demoLabel: Demo: Mae’s answers here are prewritten, not live AI
opening: Hi, I’m Mae, AgeWell’s AI helper. What’s on your mind? I can explain technology, help you think through a suspicious message, and suggest next steps. I can make mistakes, so we’ll check important information together. Please don’t share passwords, verification codes, or private account details.

starters.label: Help with my phone or computer

askAPerson.title: Ask a person
askAPerson.text: Email a person at AgeWell. Email is not emergency support, so please don’t use it if you need help right now.
askAPerson.emergency: If someone is in danger right now, call 911. If you think you’re being scammed right now, hang up and call someone you trust on a number you already know.
askAPerson.noTranscript: Your chat with Mae is not sent with your email. Nothing is shared unless you write and send the email yourself.

blocks.p: It looks like you may have typed a password, a code or an account number. Please don’t share those with me, or with anyone who calls, texts or emails you.
I didn’t save or send it, and I’ve hidden it from this chat.

steps: If you already gave a password to someone, change it using the official app or a website you type in yourself.
If you shared a bank or card number, or a code from your bank, call the number on the back of your card.
If you’re not sure what to do, talk it over with someone you trust.

blocks.p: If someone is in danger right now, call 911.
If you think you’re being scammed right now, hang up. Then call someone you trust on a number you already know.
I’m a demo helper, and email to AgeWell is not emergency support.
First, it’s not your fault. Scammers are skilled at what they do. Asking for help is a strong, smart step.

steps: If you paid, call your bank or the payment company right away. Use the number on your card or statement. Ask if they can stop or reverse the payment.
Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov, and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
If you’re 60 or older, the National Elder Fraud Hotline can help you report: 1-833-FRAUD-11 (1-833-372-8311), Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern Time.
Tell someone you trust what happened.
Watch for a second scam. Anyone who promises to “get your money back” for a fee may be a scammer, too.

blocks.p: If someone is in danger right now, call 911.
I can’t contact anyone, report anything or open accounts for you. You stay in charge.
I can’t tell you whether a voice, photo, video or message is real, and I won’t guess from how it looks or sounds.

list: A watermark is a label some AI tools add to what they make. Watermarks can be removed, and a missing watermark does not prove a person made something.
An AI detector is a program that guesses whether something was made by AI. Detectors are not definitive. They can be wrong in both directions.

blocks.p: What works better is checking a different way:

steps: Don’t reply, click or call using the message itself.
Contact the person or company using a phone number you already know or an official website you type in yourself.
Ask someone you trust to look at it with you.

blocks.note: A familiar voice is not proof of identity.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When a call sounds like someone you love and they need money fast, use the callback:

steps: Pause. Pause before sending money. Verify the request independently.
Hang up. Say, “I love you. I’ll call you right back.”
Call back on a number you already know. Use your contacts or paper list, not the number that called and not a number the caller gives you.
Can’t reach them? Call someone else you trust, even if the caller said to keep it secret.
Send nothing until you’re sure.

blocks.note: A familiar voice is not proof of identity.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A family code phrase can be a helpful extra check. It does not replace calling back.
I can’t look up or check phone numbers, and I can’t tell who is calling.

steps: Don’t call back a number from a surprise call, text, email or pop-up.
Find the number yourself: your saved contacts, the back of your card, a statement, or the company’s official website that you type in.
Call that number and ask whether the request is real.

blocks.note: Caller ID can be faked. A number that looks familiar is not proof of who is calling.
blocks.label: Good to know

blocks.p: Thank you for checking first. That’s a smart move. Let’s slow down together. I’m a demo with prewritten answers, so I can’t look at a specific message, but these steps work for most calls, texts and emails.

steps: Stop. Don’t click links, open attachments, call numbers in the message, or share codes yet.
Pause before sending money. Verify the request independently.
Find a number or website you already trust: your contacts, the back of your card, a statement, or an official website you type in yourself.
Contact the person or company that way, not through the message.
Still unsure? Talk it over with someone you trust before you act.

blocks.p: Signs to slow down: it’s urgent, it’s about money, it’s a secret, or it asks for gift cards, a wire, cryptocurrency, a payment app or a cash pickup.

blocks.note: A familiar voice is not proof of identity.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A pop-up or call saying your computer has a virus is a common trick called a tech-support scam.

steps: Don’t call the number on the screen, and don’t let anyone connect to your computer.
Close the web browser. If it won’t close, restart the computer.
If you already let someone in or paid, call your bank, and ask someone you trust to help you check the computer.
You can report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

blocks.p: Real companies don’t put phone numbers in pop-up warnings and ask you to call.
Here’s how to make text bigger. Menus differ by device and version, so yours may look a little different.

list: iPhone or iPad: open Settings, then Display & Brightness, then Text Size. Drag the slider.
Android phone or tablet: open Settings, then Display. Look for Font size, or Display size and text.
Computer web browser: hold the Ctrl key (Command on a Mac) and press the plus key to zoom in. Press Ctrl and the minus key to zoom out.

blocks.p: If yours looks different, ask someone you trust or check the official help site for your device.
An update is a free fix or improvement from the company that made your device. Updates help keep it safe.

steps: Check for updates only in your device’s Settings. On an iPhone or iPad: Settings, then General, then Software Update. On Android, look in Settings for System, then Software update. Names vary by phone.
Plug in your device and connect to Wi-Fi before you start.
Never install an “update” from a pop-up, a text, an email or a phone call.

blocks.p: Saving trusted numbers makes the callback easier on a hard day.

steps: Open your Phone or Contacts app and choose Add (often a plus sign).
Type a clear name, like “Jordan (grandson).”
Type the number you already know is right, then save.
Write the same numbers on a paper list near your phone, too.

blocks.p: Happy to help you get started. I’m a demo with prewritten tips, so I can’t see your screen or change settings for you. Which of these is closest?
Here are AgeWell’s reviewed AI & Safety Notes. For each one, I’ll show what the company announced, and separately, AgeWell’s practical guidance.
AI stands for artificial intelligence. It means computer programs that learn patterns from lots of examples. Then they use those patterns to write, talk, make pictures or answer questions.

list: AI can be useful. It can explain things, help draft a letter or read text aloud.
AI can make mistakes, and it can sound sure when it’s wrong. Check important information with a trusted source.
AI can copy voices and make fake photos and videos.
Some AI assistants can take actions, like filling out forms. Review what they’re allowed to connect to, and check before anything is submitted.

blocks.note: A familiar voice is not proof of identity.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: About me: I’m an AI helper character. On this website I’m a demonstration, so my answers are prewritten and reviewed by AgeWell, not made up on the spot.
I’m Mae, an AI helper character. I’m not a person, I’m not Dominique, and I’m not a support worker.
On this page I’m a demo with prewritten answers. For anything I can’t answer, please ask a person.
I can’t send messages, submit forms, make payments, sign you up or log in to accounts for anyone. That keeps you in charge of every Send, Submit and Pay button.
I can explain the steps, so you can do them yourself or with someone you trust.
AgeWell Innovations helps older adults and caregivers understand technology, recognize scams and build confidence through practical education. AgeWell was founded by Dominique London.
